what_its_for: Sunitinib is a cancer medicine used to treat certain types of cancer, including kidney cancer (renal cell carcinoma), a type of stomach or bowel tumor called gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) when other treatments have not worked, and a type of pancreatic cancer called pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (pNET). It works by blocking signals that help cancer cells grow and by cutting off the blood supply that tumors need to survive.
how_to_take: Take sunitinib by mouth, with or without food. Swallow the capsule whole — do not open, crush, or chew it. Try to take it at the same time each day to help you remember. If you vomit after taking your dose, do not take another dose that day — wait until your next scheduled dose.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on the type of cancer being treated and how your body responds. A common starting dose is 50 mg taken once daily for 4 weeks, followed by 2 weeks off (called a 4-weeks-on, 2-weeks-off schedule). Some patients take 37.5 mg every day without a break. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions and never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If it is already the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Do not take two doses in one day to make up for a missed dose.
storage: Store sunitinib capsules at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the bottle tightly closed and away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about proper disposal or medication take-back programs.
what_to_avoid: Avoid eating grapefruit or drinking grapefruit juice while taking sunitinib, as it can increase the amount of medicine in your blood and cause more side effects. Avoid taking St. John's Wort, a herbal supplement, as it can make sunitinib less effective. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about all medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, because many drugs can interact with sunitinib. Avoid getting pregnant while on this medicine — use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 4 weeks after your last dose. Women should not breastfeed while taking this medicine.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you experience any of the following: chest pain, shortness of breath, or swelling in your legs or ankles (signs of heart problems); unusual bleeding or bruising; severe stomach pain, vomiting, or diarrhea; signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or unusual tiredness; high blood pressure or severe headache; skin changes such as blistering, peeling, or painful sores on hands and feet; signs of low thyroid such as feeling very tired, weight gain, or feeling cold all the time; fever, chills, or signs of infection; jaw pain or tooth problems; or any sudden change in vision or speech. These may be signs of serious side effects that need immediate medical attention.
when_it_works: Sunitinib does not cure cancer, but it can slow down cancer growth and help you feel better. You may not feel any different right away. It may take several weeks before your doctor can tell if the medicine is working, usually through imaging tests or lab work. Keep taking your medicine as directed even if you do not notice any changes.
special_populations: Older adults (age 65 and over) can take sunitinib but may be more sensitive to side effects and should be monitored closely. Sunitinib is not approved for use in children. If you have liver or kidney problems, tell your doctor before starting treatment, as your dose may need to be adjusted. This medicine must not be used during pregnancy because it can harm the unborn baby. Women who could become pregnant must use reliable birth control during treatment and for at least 4 weeks after the last dose. Men with female partners who could become pregnant should also use birth control during treatment and for at least 7 weeks after the last dose.
